title: Can I use a property's cash back to clear my personal loan?
shortTitle: Cash back to clear a loan
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #249 | USING CASHBACK TO PAY PERSONAL LOAN
excerpt: A couple paying RM3,300 a month on a RM300,000 personal loan want to buy a new launch with cash back to settle it. Sean backs the swap, if the cash arrives in time.

qa.asker: Mr M, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: Mr M, 32, and his wife earn about RM15,000 a month after tax between them. In 2022 he took a RM300,000, 10-year personal loan to renovate his parents' house, now RM252,000 outstanding at RM3,300 a month, and they also pay RM2,000 rent. A new launch of about RM1 million offers a RM950,000 loan against a net price of roughly RM730,000, so buying jointly would release about RM220,000 to RM250,000 in cash back. The instalment plus maintenance would be about RM4,700, against the RM5,300 they pay now.
qa.question: Is buying a property for its cash back a sensible way to clear the personal loan?
qa.quote: In this logic, I would think that it's good.
qa.answer: Yes, in principle: it swaps a personal loan at about 8% for housing loan debt at 3% to 4%, cuts their monthly outgoings and turns rent into ownership. But first find out exactly when the developer pays the cash back, agree with his wife who carries the new instalment, and ask the bank about settling the personal loan early.

reasons.title: The type of loan decides what you pay
reasons.body: Personal loans run at about 6% to 8% and can reach 12%, and credit card balances about 16%, while his newest housing loan is at 3.85%. Sean notes that average property prices have risen about 3.6% a year over 20 years.

reasons.title: Renovation money doesn't all become value
reasons.body: Putting RM300,000 into a house doesn't add RM300,000 to its price; at most perhaps 30% to 40%, and only for approved extensions that add real space. Borrowing at personal loan rates for that is the costly part of the mistake.

reasons.title: Timing can make it a triple burden
reasons.body: Rebates are often paid with each stage of construction, but some developers only pay the cash back at handover. If so, the couple would be servicing the new loan's interest, the rent and the personal loan all at once for years.

reasons.title: It uses up his wife's borrowing power
reasons.body: He only qualifies for about RM750,000 alone, so the plan depends on her name, while she already has a house loan of her own. That limits her future purchases, so the split should be agreed openly.

actions: Ask the developer's senior management, not just the sales staff, exactly when the cash back is paid and put it in writing.
Ask the bank whether settling the RM252,000 personal loan in one lump sum earns any discount, since its interest may already be fixed.
Agree with your spouse, in writing if needed, who pays the new instalment when their name is used to qualify.
Check the rent nearby covers the instalment, as a fallback if you move or need to rent it out.
Learn how hire purchase, personal and housing loan rates are worked out before taking any new loan.
qa.caveat: Heavy rebates only appear when developers struggle to sell; in a hot market they disappear. If the cash back only comes at handover and you can't carry the overlap, the plan can make things worse rather than better.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #249. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in May 2024. The episode was sponsored by OpenHouse, a new-launch search app, and Sean mentions FAR Capital, the property investment club he is a member of, which teaches these strategies.
